headings.title: Introduction and Anatomical Pathway
headings.content: Systemic circulation is the major blood transport system that delivers oxygenated blood from the heart to every tissue in the body and returns deoxygenated blood back to the heart. This circuit begins as blood leaves the left ventricle, the thickest muscular chamber of the heart, and is forced through the aortic valve into the aorta, the largest artery in the human body. From the aorta, blood branches out into progressively smaller arteries, arterioles, and capillaries to supply the organ systems before collecting into venules and veins that ultimately drain into the superior and inferior vena cavae.

headings.title: Arterial Distribution and Capillary Exchange
headings.content: As blood travels away from the heart, elastic arteries buffer pressure changes, while muscular distribution arteries direct blood flow to specific regional beds. These vessels branch into tiny arterioles that regulate resistance and pressure before blood enters the capillary networks. Capillaries consist of a single layer of endothelial cells, making them uniquely suited for the diffusion of oxygen, carbon dioxide, glucose, and cellular wastes between the blood and interstitial fluid. Fluid movement across the capillary wall is governed by a balance between hydrostatic pressure pushing fluid out and oncotic pressure drawing fluid back in.

headings.title: Venous Return and Hemodynamics
headings.content: After passing through the capillary beds, deoxygenated blood enters venules and travels into larger veins on its journey back to the right atrium. Because venous pressure is very low, blood return relies heavily on auxiliary mechanisms: skeletal muscle contractions that squeeze deep veins, respiratory pressure changes in the thoracic cavity during breathing, and one-way valves inside medium veins that prevent backflow. Hemodynamic resistance within this entire circuit is determined by blood viscosity, vessel length, and most importantly, the radius of the blood vessels.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment of Systemic Perfusion
headings.content: Evaluating systemic perfusion requires a systematic physical and clinical examination. Nurses assess peripheral pulses for rate, rhythm, and strength to gauge left ventricular output and arterial patency. Skin color, temperature, and capillary refill time offer direct clues about microvascular blood flow to the extremities. Blood pressure measurement provides vital data regarding the hydrostatic force driving perfusion against vascular resistance. Any abnormality in these parameters can indicate early cardiovascular compromise or shock.

headings.title: Clinical Implications of Impaired Circulation
headings.content: When systemic circulation fails or becomes obstructed, tissues are deprived of adequate oxygen and nutrients, leading to cellular hypoxia and potential necrosis. Atherosclerosis, heart failure, and hypovolemic shock are common conditions that disrupt normal blood distribution. Chronic poor perfusion can cause ischemic ulcers, delayed wound healing, and organ dysfunction, particularly in metabolically active organs like the brain and kidneys. Nursing interventions focus on improving cardiac output, maintaining adequate fluid volume, and promoting vascular health through lifestyle and pharmacological support.
